newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish matadors find loophole to resume fighting.
newsitem.headline: Spanish matadors find loophole to resume fighting.

text.p: A glimmer of hope emerged on Tuesday that Spain's new bullfighting season -- paralysed by a row over illegal shaving of bulls' horns -- might go ahead.

Matadors and breeders have boycotted the bullrings in protest at new government regulations calling for dead bulls to be routinely examined after fights to see whether their horns have been shaved to reduce the danger to the matador.
Up to now, bulls have only been examined if there were suspicions the horns had indeed been illegally blunted.
Many aficionados of Spain's controversial national pastime believe the practice, which hampers the animal's distance perception, is widespread.

The row forced the cancellation of the season's first bullfights on Sunday and Monday at the Magdalena festival in the southern city of Castellon and threatens major bullfighting spectacles such as the April Fair in Seville and the prestigious San Isidro festival in Madrid in May.

But now the bullfighters have by-passed Madrid by reaching a deal with the regional government of Valencia which restores the old post-mortem rules and which they hope they will be able to repeat throughout the country.
"The problem is solved in Valencia," said Eduardo Gismera, spokesman for the Confederation of Bullfighting Professionals (CAPT) which represents most matadors, breeders and agents.
The agreement means the shows will go on at the 12-day Fallas in Valencia, the first major festival of bullfighting season, beginning on Friday.
The strike however remains in place for other regions, Gismera told Reuters.
"We will maintain the strike until we sign a similar document to the one in Valencia with other regions," he said.
Breeders face steep fines if post-morten exams show the horns were shaved and they may also be banned from fights for three months.

CAPT was initially demanding the Interior Ministry in Madrid, which controls bullfighting, change the law back to 1992 rules whereby post-mortems could only be performed on bulls which raised suspicions before a fight.
